metadata.title: Some measures of finite groups related to permutation bases

nodes.name: The derived function $f'$ (maximum over subgroups)
nodes.statement: If $f$ is a function from (isomorphism classes of) finite groups to natural numbers, let $f'$ be the function defined by \[f'(G)=\max\{f(H):H\le G\}.\]
nodes.statement_short: For a group-invariant $f$, define $f'(G)$ as the maximum of $f$ over all subgroups of $G$.
nodes.genus: a function from (isomorphism classes of) finite groups to natural numbers

nodes.name: Monotonicity characterisation of $f'$
nodes.statement: The function $f'$ is necessarily monotonic: that is, if $H\le G$, then $f'(H)\le f'(G)$. Conversely, if $f$ is monotonic, then $f=f'$; so every monotonic function is of this form.
nodes.statement_short: $f'$ is always monotonic, and the monotonic functions are exactly the functions of the form $f'$.
conclusions: if $f$ is monotonic, then $f=f'$; so every monotonic function is of this form

nodes.name: $d(G)$, the minimum number of generators
nodes.statement: An obvious function is $d(G)$, the minimum number of generators of $G$.
nodes.genus: function from finite groups to natural numbers
differentia: the minimum number of generators of $G$

nodes.name: $d(S_n)=2$
nodes.statement: Now is is well-known that $d(S_n)=2$; so this invariant is not very sensitive.

nodes.name: Babai's question: determine $d'(S_n)$
nodes.statement: Babai~\cite{babai} raised the question of determining $d'(S_n)$. The motivation was computational group theory: if we are given an arbitrary (possibly very large) subset of $S_n$, and want to know the size of the subgroup it generates, then we know that we can replace the given set by a set of size at most $d'(S_n)$ generating the same subgroup.
nodes.statement_short: Babai asked for the exact value of $d'(S_n)$, motivated by shrinking generating sets in computational group theory.

nodes.name: Algorithmic method for a minimum-size generating set
nodes.statement: This suggests that we also want, if possible, an algorithmic method for finding such a minimum-size generating set.

nodes.name: $l(G)$, the length of the longest subgroup chain
nodes.statement: Babai considered the related function $l$, where $l(G)$ is the length of the longest chain of subgroups of $G$.
differentia: $l(G)$ is the length of the longest chain of subgroups of $G$

nodes.name: $d'(G)\le l(G)$
nodes.statement: Since, obviously, $d(G)\le l(G)$, and $l$ is monotonic, (that is, $l(G)=l'(G)$), we see that $d'(G)\le l(G)$ for any group $G$.

nodes.name: Babai's bound $d'(S_n)\le l(S_n)\le 2n-1$
nodes.statement: Babai proved that \[d'(S_n)\le l(S_n)\le 2n-1.\]

nodes.name: Cameron-Solomon-Turull formula for $l(S_n)$
nodes.statement: The exact value of $S_n$ was established by Cameron, Solomon and Turull~\cite{cst}: \[l(S_n)=\left\lceil\frac{3n}{2}\right\rceil-b(n)-1,\] where $b(n)$ is the number of $1$s in the base~$2$ representation of $n$.
nodes.statement_short: The longest subgroup chain in $S_n$ has length $\lceil 3n/2\rceil - b(n) - 1$, with $b(n)$ the binary digit sum of $n$.
assumptions: $b(n)$ is the number of $1$s in the base~$2$ representation of $n$

nodes.name: Jerrum's bound $d'(S_n)\le n-1$
nodes.statement: Jerrum~\cite{jerrum} showed that $d'(S_n)\le n-1$. His proof was algorithmic: given an arbitrary set of permutations, a set of at most $n-1$ permutations generating the same subgroup can be found efficiently.
nodes.statement_short: $d'(S_n)\le n-1$, proved by an efficient algorithm that reduces any permutation set to at most $n-1$ generators.
assumptions: given an arbitrary set of permutations
conclusions: a set of at most $n-1$ permutations generating the same subgroup can be found efficiently

nodes.name: McIver-Neumann value of $d'(S_n)$
nodes.statement: The exact value of $d'(S_n)$ was established by McIver and Neumann~\cite{mn}: \[d'(S_n)=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\right\rfloor\hbox{ for }n>3.\]

nodes.name: Independent set
nodes.statement: where a set is \emph{independent} if none of its elements lies in the subgroup generated by the others
differentia: none of its elements lies in the subgroup generated by the others

nodes.name: $\mu(G)$, maximal size of an independent generating set
nodes.statement: Whiston~\cite{whiston} considered the invariant $\mu(G)$, the maximal size of an independent generating set for $G$
differentia: the maximal size of an independent generating set for $G$

nodes.name: $\mu'(G)$ is the maximum size of an independent subset
nodes.statement: Since any independent set is an independent generating set for the subgroup it generates, $\mu'(G)$ is the maximum size of an independent subset of $G$.
assumptions: any independent set is an independent generating set for the subgroup it generates
conclusions: $\mu'(G)$ is the maximum size of an independent subset of $G$

nodes.name: $\mu(G)$ in the product replacement algorithm
nodes.statement: The parameter $\mu(G)$ appears in the work of Diaconis and Saloff-Coste~\cite{ds} in the rate of convergence of the product replacement algorithm for finding a random element of a finite group.

nodes.name: Whiston's theorem: $\mu(S_n)=\mu'(S_n)=n-1$
nodes.statement: Whiston showed that \[\mu(S_n)=\mu'(S_n)=n-1.\]

nodes.name: Groups with $\mu'(G)>\mu(G)$ exist
nodes.statement: However, he observed that there are groups with $\mu'(G)>\mu(G)$.

nodes.name: Cameron-Cara classification of independent generating sets of size $n-1$
nodes.statement: Cameron and Cara~\cite{cc} found all independent generating sets of size $n-1$ in $S_n$.

nodes.name: Base for a permutation group
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a permutation group on $\Omega$. A \emph{base} for $G$ is a sequence of points of $\Omega$ whose pointwise stabiliser is the identity.
differentia: whose pointwise stabiliser is the identity

nodes.name: Bases as sequences rather than sets
nodes.statement: (Treating a base as a sequence rather than a set fits in with the use of bases in computational group theory, where the elements of a base are chosen in order.)

nodes.name: Irredundant base
nodes.statement: A base is called \emph{irredundant} if no point is fixed by the pointwise stabiliser of its predecessors
differentia: no point is fixed by the pointwise stabiliser of its predecessors

nodes.name: Minimal base
nodes.statement: it is \emph{minimal} if no point is fixed by the pointwise stabiliser of the other points in the sequence.
differentia: no point is fixed by the pointwise stabiliser of the other points in the sequence

nodes.name: Greedy construction of an irredundant base
nodes.statement: It is computationally a simple matter to choose an irredundant base; simply choose each base point to be a point moved by the stabiliser of the points previously chosen.
nodes.statement_short: Greedily extend the base by any point moved by the stabiliser of the points chosen so far.

nodes.name: Choosing a minimal base is harder
nodes.statement: It is less straightforward to choose a minimal base.

nodes.name: Minimal bases are exactly those all of whose re-orderings are irredundant
nodes.statement: Note that a base is minimal if and only if every re-ordering of it is irredundant.
conclusions: a base is minimal if and only if every re-ordering of it is irredundant

nodes.name: Maximum taken over all permutation representations
nodes.statement: In each case, the maximum is taken over all permutation representations of $G$ (not necessarily faithful).

nodes.name: $b_1(G)$
nodes.statement: $b_1(G)$ is the maximum, over all representations, of the maximum size of an irredundant base;
differentia: of the maximum size of an irredundant base

nodes.name: $b_2(G)$
nodes.statement: $b_2(G)$ is the maximum, over all representations, of the maximum size of a minimal base;
differentia: of the maximum size of a minimal base

nodes.name: $b_3(G)$
nodes.statement: $b_3(G)$ is the maximum, over all representations, of the minimum base size.

nodes.name: $\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$: the inequalities are strict
nodes.statement: These inequalities can be strict. The group $G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ has $b_1(G)=5$, $b_2(G)=4$, and $b_3(G)=3$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.2
nodes.statement: Given an irredundant base of size $b_1(G)$, the stabilisers of its initial subsequences form a properly descending chain of subgroups of length $b_1(G)$. So $b_1(G)\le l(G)$. Conversely, let \[G=G_0>G_1>\cdots>G_l=1\] be a chain of subgroups of length $l=l(G)$. Consider the action on the union of the coset spaces of the subgroups $G_i$, and let $\alpha_i$ be the point $G_i$ of the coset space $(G:G_i)$. Then $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_l)$ is an irredundant base. So $l(G)\le b_1(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Two-way inequality: stabiliser chains of an irredundant base give $b_1\le l$, and the coset action of a maximal subgroup chain gives $l\le b_1$.

nodes.name: Stabiliser chain from an irredundant base
nodes.statement: Given an irredundant base of size $b_1(G)$, the stabilisers of its initial subsequences form a properly descending chain of subgroups of length $b_1(G)$. So $b_1(G)\le l(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Turn an irredundant base into a descending subgroup chain to get $b_1(G)\le l(G)$.

nodes.name: Coset action of a maximal subgroup chain
nodes.statement: Conversely, let \[G=G_0>G_1>\cdots>G_l=1\] be a chain of subgroups of length $l=l(G)$. Consider the action on the union of the coset spaces of the subgroups $G_i$, and let $\alpha_i$ be the point $G_i$ of the coset space $(G:G_i)$. Then $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_l)$ is an irredundant base. So $l(G)\le b_1(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Build an irredundant base from a longest subgroup chain acting on the union of coset spaces, giving $l(G)\le b_1(G)$.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.3: $b_3$ of a simple group from primitive representations
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a non-abelian finite simple group. Then $b_3(G)$ can be calculated by considering only the primitive permutation representations of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: For non-abelian finite simple $G$, primitive representations suffice to compute $b_3(G)$.
assumptions: Let $G$ be a non-abelian finite simple group
conclusions: $b_3(G)$ can be calculated by considering only the primitive permutation representations of $G$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.3
nodes.statement: Given any permutation representation of $G$, we can discard fixed points, so that $G$ acts faithfully on each orbit. Now let $b_3^*(G)$ be the maximum of the minimum base sizes over all transitive representations of $G$, and suppose that there is an intransitive representation with minimum base size greater than $b_3^*(G)$. Now there exist at most $b_3^*(G)$ points in an orbit whose stabiliser acts trivially on that orbit, and hence is trivial (since the action on the orbit is faithful), contrary to assumption. Now let $b_3^+(G)$ be the maximum of the minimum base sizes over all primitive representations of $G$, and suppose that there is a transitive but imprimitive representation with base size greater than $b_3^+(G)$. There are at most $b_3^+(G)$ maximal blocks whose stabiliser acts trivially on the block system, and hence is trivial (since again the action is faithful), contrary to assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Two successive reductions by contradiction: intransitive to transitive, then imprimitive to primitive, using faithfulness on orbits and blocks.

nodes.name: Discard fixed points to get faithful orbit actions
nodes.statement: Given any permutation representation of $G$, we can discard fixed points, so that $G$ acts faithfully on each orbit.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to representations acting faithfully on each orbit.

nodes.name: Intransitive representations reduce to transitive ones
nodes.statement: Now let $b_3^*(G)$ be the maximum of the minimum base sizes over all transitive representations of $G$, and suppose that there is an intransitive representation with minimum base size greater than $b_3^*(G)$. Now there exist at most $b_3^*(G)$ points in an orbit whose stabiliser acts trivially on that orbit, and hence is trivial (since the action on the orbit is faithful), contrary to assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Assume an intransitive representation beats $b_3^*(G)$ and contradict it via a small base inside one orbit.

nodes.name: Imprimitive representations reduce to primitive ones
nodes.statement: Now let $b_3^+(G)$ be the maximum of the minimum base sizes over all primitive representations of $G$, and suppose that there is a transitive but imprimitive representation with base size greater than $b_3^+(G)$. There are at most $b_3^+(G)$ maximal blocks whose stabiliser acts trivially on the block system, and hence is trivial (since again the action is faithful), contrary to assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Same contradiction one level up, using maximal blocks instead of points.

nodes.name: $\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ on points and lines: Proposition 2.3 fails for $b_2$
nodes.statement: This proposition does not hold for $b_2(G)$. For the group $G=\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)\cong\mathrm{PSL}(3,2)$, a minimal base in any transitive representation has size at most $3$. However, in the action on the points and lines of the projective plane of order~$2$, there is a minimal base of size~$4$, consisting of two points and two lines such that each point lies on one of the lines and each line passes through one of the points.
nodes.statement_short: An intransitive point-line action of $\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ has a minimal base of size 4, beating every transitive representation.

nodes.name: The subgroup lattice $L(G)$
nodes.statement: The subgroups of the group $G$ form a lattice $L(G)$, with the operations $H\wedge K=H\cap K$ and $H\vee K=\langle H,K\rangle$.
differentia: with the operations $H\wedge K=H\cap K$ and $H\vee K=\langle H,K\rangle$

nodes.name: Meet-semilattice of $L(G)$
nodes.statement: A \emph{meet-semilattice} of $L(G)$ is a collection of subgroups containing $G$ and closed under $\wedge$

nodes.name: Join-semilattice of $L(G)$
nodes.statement: while a \emph{join-semilattice} is a collection of subgroups containing the trivial group $1$ and closed under $\vee$.

nodes.name: The Boolean lattice $B(n)$
nodes.statement: The \emph{Boolean lattice} $B(n)$ is the lattice of subsets of an $n$-set.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.1: meet-embeddability iff join-embeddability of $B(n)$
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group. Then $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice in $L(G)$ if and only if it is embeddable as a join-semilattice.
nodes.statement_short: $B(n)$ embeds in the subgroup lattice as a meet-semilattice exactly when it embeds as a join-semilattice.
conclusions: $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice in $L(G)$ if and only if it is embeddable as a join-semilattice

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $B(n)$ is a join-semilattice of $L(G)$. Let $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then, for every subset $I$ of $N$, there is a subgroup $H_I$ of $G$, and $H_{I\cup J}=\langle H_i,H_j\rangle$ for any two subsets $I$ and $J$. Moreover, all these subgroups are distinct. In particular, $H_i\not\le H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$ for all $i$ (where $H_i$ is shorthand for $H_{\{i\}}$); else \[H_N=\langle H_i,H_{N\setminus\{i\}}\rangle=H_{N\setminus\{i\}},\] contrary to assumption. Let $K_i=H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$, and for any $I\subseteq N$, put \[K_I=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i,\] with the convention that $K_\emptyset=G$. We claim that all the subgroups $K_i$ are distinct. Suppose that two of them are equal, say $K_I=K_J$. By interchanging $I$ and $J$ if necessary, we may assume that there exists $i\in I\setminus J$. But then $H_i\le K_J$ while $H_i\not\le K_I$, a contradiction. Now it is clear that $K_J\cap K_J=K_{I\cap J}$, so we have an embedding of $B(n)$ as a meet-semilattice (where we have reversed the order-isomoprhism to simplify the notation). The reverse implication is proved by an almost identical argument.
nodes.statement_short: From a join-embedding, complement the index sets ($K_i=H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$) to build a meet-embedding, proving distinctness by contradiction; the converse is symmetric.

nodes.name: Set up the join-semilattice and non-containment
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $B(n)$ is a join-semilattice of $L(G)$. Let $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then, for every subset $I$ of $N$, there is a subgroup $H_I$ of $G$, and $H_{I\cup J}=\langle H_i,H_j\rangle$ for any two subsets $I$ and $J$. Moreover, all these subgroups are distinct. In particular, $H_i\not\le H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$ for all $i$ (where $H_i$ is shorthand for $H_{\{i\}}$); else \[H_N=\langle H_i,H_{N\setminus\{i\}}\rangle=H_{N\setminus\{i\}},\] contrary to assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a join-embedding $I\mapsto H_I$ and derive $H_i\not\le H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$.

nodes.name: Define the candidate meet-semilattice $K_I$
nodes.statement: Let $K_i=H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$, and for any $I\subseteq N$, put \[K_I=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i,\] with the convention that $K_\emptyset=G$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the complemented subgroups $K_i$ and their intersections $K_I$.

nodes.name: The subgroups $K_I$ are distinct
nodes.statement: We claim that all the subgroups $K_i$ are distinct. Suppose that two of them are equal, say $K_I=K_J$. By interchanging $I$ and $J$ if necessary, we may assume that there exists $i\in I\setminus J$. But then $H_i\le K_J$ while $H_i\not\le K_I$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Prove distinctness of the $K_I$ by contradiction using an index in $I\setminus J$.

nodes.name: Conclude the meet-semilattice embedding
nodes.statement: Now it is clear that $K_J\cap K_J=K_{I\cap J}$, so we have an embedding of $B(n)$ as a meet-semilattice (where we have reversed the order-isomoprhism to simplify the notation).
nodes.statement_short: Closure under intersection gives the meet-semilattice embedding (with reversed order).

nodes.name: Reverse implication
nodes.statement: The reverse implication is proved by an almost identical argument.
nodes.statement_short: The converse direction follows by the dual argument.

nodes.name: Semilattice embeddability is weaker than lattice embeddability
nodes.statement: Note that the conditions of the proposition are not equivalent to embeddability of $B(n)$ as a lattice.

nodes.name: Quaternion group of order 8 and $B(2)$
nodes.statement: For example, if $G$ is the quaternion group of order $8$, then $B(2)$ is embeddable as both a meet-semilattice and a join-semilattice but not as a lattice.

nodes.name: Proposition 3.2: $\mu'(G)$ and $b_2(G)$ as maximal Boolean semilattice ranks
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group. \begin{enumerate} \item The largest $n$ such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a join-semilattice of $L(G)$ is $\mu'(G)$. \item The largest $n$ such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice of $L(G)$ in such a way that the minimal element is a normal subgroup of $G$ is $b_2(G)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\mu'(G)$ is the largest Boolean join-semilattice rank in $L(G)$; $b_2(G)$ is the largest meet-semilattice rank with normal minimal element.
conclusions: The largest $n$ such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a join-semilattice of $L(G)$ is $\mu'(G)$
The largest $n$ such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice of $L(G)$ in such a way that the minimal element is a normal subgroup of $G$ is $b_2(G)$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement: (a) Let $\{g_1,\ldots,g_n\}$ be an independent set in $G$, where $n=\mu'(G)$. Let $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $H_I=\langle g_i:i\in I\rangle$ form a join-semilattice of $G$ isomorphic to $B(n)$. Conversely, suppose that we have a join-semilattice given by the subgroups $H_I$ for $I\subseteq N$. Choose $g_i\notin H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$. Then clearly the elements $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ are independent. \smallskip (b) Let $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ be a minimal base for $G$ in some permutation representation. Let $K_i$ be the stabiliser of $\alpha_i$, and $K_I=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i$ for $I\subseteq N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $K_I$ form a meet-semilattice of $G$. The subgroup$ K_N$ is the kernel of the permutation representation (by definition of a base), and so is a normal subgroup of $G$. Conversely, suppose that we have a meet-semilattice given by the subgroups $K_I$ for $I\subseteq N$, such that $K_N$ is a normal subgroup fo $G$; the notation is chosen so that $K_I\cap K_J=K_{I\cup J}$. Now consider the permutation representation on the union of the coset spaces of the subgroups $K_i=K_{\{i\}}$. Since the intersection of all these subgroups is normal, it is the kernel of the representation, and the points corresponding to the subgroups $K_i$ form a base. It is minimal, since the intersection of fewer than $n$ of the subgroups is not equal to $K_N$.
nodes.statement_short: Both parts are two-way constructions: independent sets ↔ Boolean join-semilattices of generated subgroups, and minimal bases ↔ Boolean meet-semilattices of point stabilisers with normal minimal element.

nodes.name: Part (a): independent set gives a join-semilattice
nodes.statement: (a) Let $\{g_1,\ldots,g_n\}$ be an independent set in $G$, where $n=\mu'(G)$. Let $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $H_I=\langle g_i:i\in I\rangle$ form a join-semilattice of $G$ isomorphic to $B(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Build $B(n)$ as a join-semilattice from a maximum independent set.

nodes.name: Part (a) converse: join-semilattice gives an independent set
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that we have a join-semilattice given by the subgroups $H_I$ for $I\subseteq N$. Choose $g_i\notin H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$. Then clearly the elements $g_1,\ldots,g_n$ are independent.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $g_i$ outside $H_{N\setminus\{i\}}$ to recover an independent set.

nodes.name: Part (b): minimal base gives a meet-semilattice with normal minimum
nodes.statement: (b) Let $(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)$ be a minimal base for $G$ in some permutation representation. Let $K_i$ be the stabiliser of $\alpha_i$, and $K_I=\bigcap_{i\in I}K_i$ for $I\subseteq N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Then the subgroups $K_I$ form a meet-semilattice of $G$. The subgroup$ K_N$ is the kernel of the permutation representation (by definition of a base), and so is a normal subgroup of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Point stabilisers of a minimal base form a Boolean meet-semilattice whose minimum is the kernel, hence normal.

nodes.name: Part (b) converse: meet-semilattice gives a minimal base
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that we have a meet-semilattice given by the subgroups $K_I$ for $I\subseteq N$, such that $K_N$ is a normal subgroup fo $G$; the notation is chosen so that $K_I\cap K_J=K_{I\cup J}$. Now consider the permutation representation on the union of the coset spaces of the subgroups $K_i=K_{\{i\}}$. Since the intersection of all these subgroups is normal, it is the kernel of the representation, and the points corresponding to the subgroups $K_i$ form a base. It is minimal, since the intersection of fewer than $n$ of the subgroups is not equal to $K_N$.
nodes.statement_short: The coset action of the $K_i$ has the $K_i$-points as a minimal base.

nodes.name: Corollary 3.3: $b_2(G)\le\mu'(G)$
nodes.statement: $b_2(G)\le\mu'(G)$ for any group $G$.

nodes.name: Is $b_2(G)<\mu'(G)$ possible? (normal minimal element question)
nodes.statement: I do not know a group where the inequality is strict. Resolving this is equivalent to the following question. Let $n$ be maximal such that $B(n)$ is embeddable as a meet-semilattice of $L(G)$. Is there an embedding of $B(n)$ for which the minimal element is normal?
nodes.statement_short: Is $b_2(G)=\mu'(G)$ always? Equivalently, can a maximal Boolean meet-semilattice always be chosen with normal minimal element?

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.4
nodes.statement: We have \[n-1\le b_3(S_n)\le b_2(S_n)\le \mu'(S_n)=n-1,\] wwhere the first inequality holds because any base in the natural representation has size $n-1$; the second is trivial; the third comes from the preceding Corollary; and the equality is Whiston's theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $b_3(S_n)$ and $b_2(S_n)$ between $n-1$ and $\mu'(S_n)=n-1$ using Corollary 3.3 and Whiston's theorem.

nodes.name: The sandwich chain
nodes.statement: We have \[n-1\le b_3(S_n)\le b_2(S_n)\le \mu'(S_n)=n-1,\]
nodes.statement_short: Set up the chain of inequalities pinning both measures to $n-1$.

nodes.name: First inequality: natural representation
nodes.statement: wwhere the first inequality holds because any base in the natural representation has size $n-1$
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound $n-1\le b_3(S_n)$ from the natural representation of $S_n$.

nodes.name: Second inequality is trivial
nodes.statement: the second is trivial
nodes.statement_short: $b_3\le b_2$ holds by Proposition 2.1.

nodes.name: Third inequality from the preceding Corollary
nodes.statement: the third comes from the preceding Corollary
nodes.statement_short: $b_2\le\mu'$ by Corollary 3.3.

nodes.name: Final equality from Whiston's theorem
nodes.statement: and the equality is Whiston's theorem
nodes.statement_short: $\mu'(S_n)=n-1$ by Whiston's theorem.
